questions.question: Why might a requirements author add tables or graphical models to natural language requirements?

options.A: To replace all textual descriptions with visuals
options.B: To show how computations proceed, system state changes, and user interactions
options.C: To increase the length of the documentation without adding value
options.D: To comply with a mandatory industry standard unrelated to clarity

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] Adding tables or graphical models helps illustrate computations, state changes, and user interactions, as described on [Page 24].

---

questions.question: Which of the following can serve as the additional graphical information for a use case besides a textual description?

options.C: UML sequence diagram or state chart (or both)

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The text states that additional information may be a textual description or one or more graphical models such as the UML sequence or state charts [Page 25].

---

questions.question: In a high‑level use case diagram, how is an actor visually represented?
questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] Actors are depicted as stick figures in use case diagrams [Page 25].

---

questions.question: In a use case diagram, what does a named ellipse denote?

options.C: A class of interaction (the use case)

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] Each class of interaction is represented as a named ellipse, i.e., a use case [Page 25].

---

questions.question: According to the description, what constitutes the simplest form of a use case?

options.A: Identification of the actors involved and the name of the interaction
options.B: Actors, interaction name, and a full textual scenario description
options.C: Actors, interaction name, and a UML sequence diagram
options.D: Actors, interaction name, and implementation code snippets

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The simplest form identifies actors and names the interaction, with additional details added later [Page 25].

---

questions.question: The tabular specification shown for an insulin pump primarily illustrates which aspect of the system?

options.B: Computation steps of the pump’s operation

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] The table is used to specify the computation performed by the insulin pump, as indicated on [Page 24].

---

questions.question: Why did use cases become a fundamental feature of the Unified Modeling Language (UML)?

options.A: Because they were first introduced in the Objectory method
options.B: Because they describe interactions between users and a system
options.C: Because they eliminate the need for any textual requirements
options.D: Because they are only useful for low‑level coding details

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] Use cases describe user‑system interactions, which is why they are central to UML [Page 25].

---

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the purpose of incorporating tables or graphical models into requirements documentation?

options.B: They illustrate how computations proceed and how the system state changes.
options.C: They are solely for documenting hardware specifications.
options.D: They are optional and rarely improve stakeholder understanding.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] Tables and graphical models help show computation flow, state changes, and interaction sequences [Page 24].

---

questions.question: How are actors connected to use cases in a use case diagram?

options.C: With arrows pointing from actor to use case

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] Lines (solid) link actors with the interactions they participate in [Page 25].

---

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a possible form of additional information for a use case?
questions.explanation: [Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] The context mentions textual description, UML sequence, and state charts, but not source code, as additional information for a use case [Page 25].
